title: When the biggest coin is wrong
hook: Grab the biggest coin each time and you get the fewest coins. Usually.

doesNotKnow: that taking the biggest option each step can miss the best total

misconception: Grabbing the best-looking option at each step always gives the best total.
objective: The learner can explain that with coins 1, 3 and 4, taking the biggest coin first makes 6 as 4 + 1 + 1 (3 coins) while 3 + 3 needs 2, because the early big coin leaves a remainder only small coins can fill; and that greedy is right for some targets and coin sets.

claims.text: With coins 1, 3 and 4, the fewest coins that make 6 is 2 (3 + 3).
claims.source: Exhaustive dynamic-programming search over all combinations (builder ran it in Node): best(6) = 2. No single coin is 6, so 2 is the minimum.

claims.text: Taking the biggest coin that fits each time makes 6 as 4 + 1 + 1, which is 3 coins.
claims.source: Greedy: 6 - 4 = 2, then 1, then 1. Builder ran it in Node.

claims.text: For 8, greedy takes 4 + 4, the best possible; for 10 it takes 4 + 4 + 1 + 1 (4 coins) where 4 + 3 + 3 needs 3.
claims.source: Builder ran greedy and exhaustive search for targets 1..12 with coins {1, 3, 4}: greedy is worse only at 6 (3 vs 2) and 10 (4 vs 3).

claims.text: With coins 1, 5, 10 and 25, taking the biggest coin first always gives the fewest coins.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed., Problem 16-1(a) (greedy is optimal for quarters, dimes, nickels and pennies); Kozen and Zaks, 'Optimal bounds for the change-making problem', TCS 123 (1994). Builder also checked every amount 1..1,000 in Node against exhaustive search: all equal.

claims.text: With coins 1, 5 and 6, greedy makes 10 as 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, while 5 + 5 needs only 2 coins.
claims.source: Greedy: 10 - 6 = 4, and only 1s fit 4, giving 5 coins. 5 + 5 = 10 with 2 coins; no single coin is 10, so 2 is the minimum.

recall.question: Coins are worth 1, 5 and 6. Greedy makes 10 as 6 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1. Is that the fewest coins?
options: Yes: always take the biggest coin
recall.why: Taking the 6 leaves 4, which only 1s can fill. Two 5s make 10 with 2 coins: the greedy first step blocked the better answer.
